title: Plantain salve for minor wounds
subtitle: A shelf-ready salve for minor cuts, grazes, and insect bites
excerpt: A two-stage preparation: dried plantain leaf infused into olive oil at 60-65°C, then combined with beeswax at a 1:4 ratio to set into a firm salve. Traditionally applied to minor cuts, grazes, and insect bites for ongoing wound care. Makes approximately 100 g of salve, which keeps for 12 months.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), Plantain (Plantago major) entry : vulnerary and wound-healing uses. King's American Dispensatory (Felter and Lloyd, 1898), Plantago section. Traditional western herbal preparation ratios: infused oil 1:5 herb to oil by weight; salve 1:4 beeswax to oil by weight.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Salve keeps for 12 months in a sealed tin in a cool dark place. Prepare in a single session using the double-boiler oil method.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Store in a sealed tin in a cool dark place. Discard if the surface develops white spots or the salve smells rancid.

glossaryTerms.definition: An oil in which dried plant material has been gently heated to extract the herb's active constituents into the oil base.
A firm, spreadable preparation made by combining an infused or plain oil with melted beeswax. Sets at room temperature to a solid that softens on skin contact.

content.text: Plantain salve is a firm, shelf-ready preparation made in two stages: dried Plantago major leaf is first infused into olive oil at 60-65°C for 2-4 hours, then combined with melted beeswax at a 1:4 ratio by weight to set into a
salve
. Traditionally applied to minor cuts, grazes, and insect bites to support wound care over the following days. The finished salve keeps for 12 months in a sealed tin.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body:
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.

Plantain (Plantago major) has no significant safety flags for external use at these preparation levels. Patch-test on a small area of skin before first use if you have sensitive skin.

This remedy is for minor surface wounds only. See the red flags section below for wounds that need medical attention.

Paediatric use: external application of this salve is generally well tolerated in children, but consult a paediatric doctor or herbalist for use on infants under six months.

content.text: Ingredients
Method
Stage 1: Make the infused oil
Place 20 g of dried plantain leaf and 100 ml of olive oil into the top vessel of a double boiler. Stir to combine.

Heat the double boiler over a low flame. Use a probe thermometer to hold the oil at 60-65°C. Maintain this temperature for 2-4 hours, checking every 30 minutes. The oil should turn a pale green-yellow and smell of plantain.
Remove from the heat and leave to cool for 10 minutes. Strain through muslin cloth into a measuring jug, squeezing the cloth to extract all the oil. You should have approximately 80-90 ml of
infused oil
Stage 2: Make the salve
Return the infused oil to the clean double boiler. Add 25 g of beeswax pellets.
Warm gently over the double boiler, stirring, until all the beeswax has melted. The mixture should be fluid and clear.
To check the set, drop a small amount onto a cold saucer. It should firm up within a minute. If it is too soft, melt in a little more beeswax; if too hard, add a little more oil.
Pour the molten salve into clean salve tins or small jars. Leave undisturbed for 30 minutes to set fully before lidding.
Dosing

Apply a thin layer to the cleaned wound or bite, once or twice a day. Use for up to seven days on a minor cut or graze. For insect bites, apply as needed to the affected area until resolved, up to four times a day.
Storage

Store in a sealed tin or jar in a cool dark place. The salve keeps for 12 months. Discard if the surface develops white spots or the salve smells rancid. Always use clean fingers or a spatula to avoid contaminating the tin.
When not to use this remedy

See a doctor or A&E for deep cuts, cuts that will not stop bleeding after fifteen minutes of pressure. Cuts over a joint, cuts on the face or hand with possible nerve or tendon involvement, animal or human bites, or any wound showing spreading redness, warmth, pus, or fever. These are signs of infection that need medical treatment.
Call 999 for any sign of anaphylaxis from a sting: swollen lips or tongue, difficulty breathing, dizziness, or sudden generalised rash. See A&E for tick bites with a bullseye rash.
